<reason>A superb, close debate. B wins because its core route survived intact: it cleanly demolished A's "earnings are already legible" premise (a 1099 is an annual gross tax form, not contemporaneous UI wage reporting), answered the "records can't show why" objection with existing quit-vs-layoff adjudication plus richer platform data, and — most decisively — neutralized A's capture argument by noting the motion's text contains no safe harbor and that contemporaneous earnings records arm misclassification plaintiffs, a reversal A never directly rebutted. B also answered both pressure questions head-on, including an honest refusal on the purity pledge. A's case was analytically deep and rhetorically brilliant (payer-written logs, gross-vs-net erosion of "working always pays more," the narrow claimable set, and a devastating closing takedown of B's van image as an injury case UI never reaches). But A sidestepped B's Q2 entirely — no timeline for the classification alternative, no answer to why dual-track is impossible — leaving its remedy as "someday," and suffered two clipped turns. A's heavy blows damaged B's framing more than its mechanism.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's paired strikes: B2.1's 1099 demolition (removing A's foundational "legibility was never the problem" claim) and B4.3–4.4's "this motion doesn't foreclose the classification fight — it arms it," which flipped A's strongest political-economy argument. A's best counter-blow was the closing exposure that B's signature injured-driver image is an availability-failing case UI never covered — sharp, but too late to reach B's deactivation/demand-collapse core.</best_rebuttal>
